params.question: A tibial fracture has healed with suspected rotational deformity. Standard AP and lateral radiographs show angulation but the degree of rotation cannot be quantified. Which investigation resolves this limitation?

answers.text: Repeat radiographs with the limb internally rotated

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Repositioning the limb for radiographs does not permit accurate rotational measurement. Quantifying rotation requires comparing the cross-sectional anatomy at the fracture site with the bone ends, which plain films cannot do regardless of limb position.

CT with 3D reconstruction defines the exact angle of rotation by comparing the cross-section of the bone at the fracture site with its proximal and distal ends — precisely the measurement plain X-rays cannot provide.

answers.text: MRI of the fracture site with coronal sequences

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MRI excels at soft-tissue assessment (cartilage, ligaments, marrow oedema) but is not the standard investigation for quantifying rotational bony malunion. CT scanogram is the modality of choice.

answers.text: Standing full-length radiograph of both lower limbs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Standing full-length films measure mechanical axis deviation and overall limb alignment, but they remain plain radiographs and still cannot accurately quantify rotational deformity at the fracture site.

overallFeedback.feedback: Plain X-rays cannot measure true rotational malunion. A CT scanogram with 3D reconstruction is needed because it compares the cross-sectional anatomy of the bone at the fracture site with its ends, directly quantifying the degree of twist.

Correct. Plain X-rays show angulation and shortening well, but rotational malunion can only be accurately measured by CT scanogram, which compares cross-sectional bone anatomy above and below the fracture site.

interactions.label: A 40-year-old patient presents with a tibial non-union showing abundant callus f

params.question: A 40-year-old patient presents with a tibial non-union showing abundant callus formation at the fracture site but persistent abnormal motion. Which management approach is most appropriate?

answers.text: Iliac crest autologous bone graft with compression plating

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bone graft provides osteogenic cells, osteoinductive proteins, and an osteoconductive scaffold — components needed when biology has failed (atrophic non-union). Here, abundant callus confirms the biology is intact; the deficit is mechanical stability.

This staged protocol is reserved for infected non-union, where dead tissue and bacteria must be cleared before reconstruction can proceed. Hypertrophic non-union with abundant callus does not follow this pathway.

Abundant callus indicates hypertrophic non-union — biology is intact but stability is lacking. Reamed intramedullary nailing provides rigid fixation while also stimulating intramedullary blood vessel growth and releasing local growth factors.

answers.text: Recombinant bone morphogenetic protein injection with splinting

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: BMPs address a biological deficiency and are used as adjuncts in atrophic non-union. Here the biology is already robust (abundant callus), and splinting alone does not provide the rigid fixation that hypertrophic non-union requires.

overallFeedback.feedback: Abundant callus = hypertrophic non-union, meaning the biology is intact but stability is poor. The treatment is rigid mechanical fixation alone — intramedullary nailing with reaming for the tibia and femur. Bone graft is reserved for atrophic non-union where biology has failed.

Correct. Abundant callus at a non-union site is the hallmark of hypertrophic non-union — the biology is working but mechanical stability is insufficient. Rigid fixation alone (preferably IM nailing with reaming for long bones) is the treatment.

interactions.label: The final Gustilo-Anderson grade of an open fracture should be assigned in the e

params.question: The final Gustilo-Anderson grade of an open fracture should be assigned in the emergency department at initial presentation.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: The final Gustilo-Anderson grade should be assigned in the operating theatre after thorough debridement, not at initial ED presentation. Emergency department assessment systematically underestimates the grade because devitalised tissue obscures the true extent of damage — wounds initially appearing Grade II often prove to be Grade IIIA or IIIB once properly explored.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The final grade must be assigned in the operating theatre after thorough debridement. Wounds that appear Grade II in the ED frequently turn out to be Grade IIIA or IIIB once devitalised tissue is removed and the true extent of soft-tissue damage and contamination becomes visible.

interactions.label: A motorcyclist with a Gustilo Grade IIIA open tibial fracture arrives in the eme

params.question: A motorcyclist with a Gustilo Grade IIIA open tibial fracture arrives in the emergency department. Which antibiotic regimen should be initiated within the first hour?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A first-generation cephalosporin alone (e.g. cefazolin) is adequate only for Grade I and Grade II open fractures. Grade III wounds carry a much higher infection risk and require broader gram-negative coverage in addition.

Grade III open fractures require a first-generation cephalosporin (e.g. cefazolin for gram-positive cover) plus an aminoglycoside (e.g. gentamicin for gram-negative cover). High-dose penicillin is added if there is soil/farm contamination or a vascular injury.
Aminoglycosides provide gram-negative coverage but lack adequate gram-positive cover. They are never used as monotherapy for open fractures; they are always combined with a cephalosporin.

Carbapenems are reserve antibiotics used for resistant organisms and are not part of the standard empirical regimen for open fractures. Their indiscriminate use promotes resistance without improving outcomes over the guideline regimen.

overallFeedback.feedback: Grade III open fractures require a first-generation cephalosporin (gram-positive cover) plus an aminoglycoside (gram-negative cover), started within one hour. This 1-hour window replaces the older 6-hour debridement rule, because bacteria begin forming biofilms on damaged tissue within minutes of injury.

Correct. Grade III open fractures require combined antibiotic therapy — a first-generation cephalosporin plus an aminoglycoside — initiated within one hour of presentation, before bacteria can form a protective biofilm on damaged tissue.

interactions.label: A 6-year-old with a displaced extension-type supracondylar fracture cannot form

params.question: A 6-year-old with a displaced extension-type supracondylar fracture cannot form the OK sign (tip-to-tip thumb–index pinch) but has completely normal sensation throughout the hand. Which structure is most likely injured?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ulnar nerve injury causes numbness over the little finger and ulnar half of the ring finger, plus weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles. This patient's sensation is entirely normal, ruling out ulnar nerve involvement.

The anterior interosseous nerve is a pure motor branch of the median nerve. Its injury paralyses flexor pollicis longus and the index finger's flexor digitorum profundus, abolishing the tip-to-tip OK sign pinch while preserving all sensation — exactly this clinical picture.
A complete median nerve trunk injury would also cause numbness over the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger, plus thenar weakness. Normal sensation here rules out the main trunk.

The posterior interosseous nerve is a motor branch of the radial nerve that supplies wrist and finger extensors. Its injury causes wrist drop and finger drop — not a loss of the flexion-based OK sign.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key finding is a motor-only deficit (failed OK sign) with intact sensation. This pattern points to the anterior interosseous nerve — a pure motor branch of the median nerve and the most commonly injured nerve in supracondylar fractures. A median trunk injury would also cause sensory loss; ulnar and radial nerve injuries produce different motor patterns.

Correct. The anterior interosseous nerve is the most commonly injured nerve in extension-type supracondylar fractures. Being a pure motor branch, its palsy produces inability to flex the thumb IP and index DIP joints (failed OK sign) with completely preserved sensation.
